exercises.title: 研究室見学への問い合わせ
exercises.subject: Request to visit a research laboratory
exercises.context: You are taking a university preparatory course and would like to learn about research in an engineering laboratory. Write to a faculty member to ask about a short visit. This is an imagined practice situation.
requirements: Introduce your course status and explain your interest in the laboratory.
Suggest two possible times: Wednesday after 2 p.m. or Friday before noon.
Ask whether a short visit is possible and whether any preparation is required.
exercises.modelAnswer:
Dear Dr. Taylor,

I am currently taking the university preparatory course, and I am interested in learning how engineering research connects theory with practical experiments. I would be grateful for an opportunity to visit your laboratory briefly and learn about its work.

I am available on Wednesday after 2 p.m. or Friday before noon. Would either of these times be convenient for a short visit? If a visit is possible, could you also let me know whether I should read any introductory material or complete any formalities beforehand?

Thank you for considering my request. I understand that the laboratory may have limited availability, and I would be happy to follow any arrangements you suggest.

Best regards,
Alex Morgan
explanation: The email identifies the learner as a preparatory-course participant, gives a clear academic reason, and proposes exactly the two permitted time windows. It asks rather than assumes that laboratory access is available.
The final question asks about both reading and formal arrangements before the visit. This makes the request practical without inventing a confirmed invitation.

phrases: Would either of these times be convenient? — いずれかの時間はご都合がよいでしょうか。

exercises.title: 静かな自習席と共同作業室
exercises.context: A university has funding to improve its library. Should it prioritise quiet individual study spaces or rooms for group work? Explain your position.

posts.name: Ana
posts.text: Group rooms should come first because students need to practise presentations and solve problems together. A library can offer equipment and space that students may not have at home.

posts.name: Luis
posts.text: Quiet individual spaces are more important. Students can often talk elsewhere, but finding somewhere to concentrate without interruptions can be difficult.

requirements: State and support your preferred funding priority.
Respond meaningfully to both Ana and Luis.
Develop a concrete example or proposal in at least 100 words.
exercises.modelAnswer: I would prioritise quiet individual spaces, while using a smaller part of the budget to improve existing group rooms. Luis makes a strong point: students who share a noisy home may have few alternatives when they need to read or write carefully. However, Ana is also right that group projects require suitable space and equipment. Instead of treating the two needs as completely separate, the university could first measure demand at different times of day. For example, if quiet desks are consistently full but group rooms are empty in the morning, some rooms could be available for silent study during those hours. Clear booking rules would preserve them for collaborative work later. This approach would give priority to concentration without ignoring students who need to rehearse presentations together.
explanation: The response chooses quiet spaces as the priority, accepts the need for group work, and proposes collecting demand information rather than assuming one universal solution.
The morning-room example is hypothetical. It explains how a policy could satisfy Luis’s concentration concern and Ana’s collaboration concern within a limited budget.
prioritiseは優先する、collaborative workは共同作業です。仮定の具体例であり、実在する大学の利用率を主張していません。
phrases: measure demand — 需要を測定する
without ignoring … — 〜を無視せずに
exercises.answerBasis: Original practice exercise; answer and explanation reviewed editorially. 解答・解説は編集作成。

exercises.title: 録画講義と出席
exercises.context: Should universities record every lecture and allow students to decide whether to attend in person? Explain your position.

posts.name: Nora
posts.text: Every lecture should be recorded. Recordings help students review difficult material and support those who are ill or have unavoidable timetable conflicts.

posts.name: Daniel
posts.text: Automatic recording may reduce attendance and participation. A live class lets students ask questions immediately and learn from one another.

requirements: State and support your policy on lecture recording and attendance.
Respond meaningfully to both Nora and Daniel.
Develop a concrete safeguard or example in at least 100 words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Universities should record most lectures, but access to recordings should support rather than replace participation. Nora is right that recordings are valuable when students are ill and when a complex explanation needs to be reviewed. However, Daniel's concern is also important because students can lose the habit of preparing questions if attendance becomes optional without limits. A reasonable policy would keep seminars and laboratory sessions in person while recording large lectures. Students could use the recording freely after attending, whereas those who miss class repeatedly might need to explain the reason to an adviser. For example, a student recovering from influenza could continue learning without putting classmates at risk. This approach improves access while preserving the interaction that makes live teaching useful.
explanation: The response takes a qualified position, directly addresses access and participation, and proposes a distinction between large lectures and interactive sessions.
The illness example explains when recording adds genuine value; it does not claim that every absence should be treated identically.
safeguardは『悪影響を防ぐ仕組み』、qualified positionは『条件付きの立場』です。これは方針を論じる架空の練習です。
phrases: support rather than replace — 置き換えるのではなく支える
preserve interaction — 相互交流を維持する
exercises.answerBasis: Original practice exercise; answer and explanation reviewed editorially. 解答・解説は編集作成。

exercises.context: You missed a compulsory field visit because you were ill. Write to the course coordinator. This is an imagined practice situation.
requirements: Identify the field-visit group and date, and briefly explain why you were absent.
Ask whether you should join the next visit or complete an alternative assignment.
Ask for the relevant deadline and any material you should review.
exercises.modelAnswer:
Dear Dr. Morgan,

I am writing about the geology field visit for Group B on 21 October. I was unable to attend because I was ill that morning and did not want to risk passing the illness to other students.

Could you please let me know whether I should join the next available visit or complete an alternative assignment? I would be willing to do either option so that I can cover the missed learning outcomes.

I would also be grateful if you could confirm the relevant deadline and tell me whether there are any notes, maps or safety instructions I should review beforehand.

Thank you for your guidance.

Best regards,
Alex Morgan
explanation: The email identifies the exact imagined session, gives a concise reason, and asks for guidance instead of assuming which replacement option is permitted.
The final request covers both the deadline and preparation material, satisfying the third requirement without adding unverifiable details.
learning outcomesは『学習到達目標』、relevant deadlineは『該当する締切』です。日付・氏名・授業は架空設定です。
phrases: Could you please let me know whether …? — 〜かどうか教えていただけますか。
cover the missed learning outcomes — 欠席分の学習目標を補う

exercises.title: 全学生向けデータリテラシー
exercises.context: Should every first-year university student be required to take a basic data-literacy course, regardless of their major? Explain your position.

posts.name: Sara
posts.text: A required course would help students judge graphs, surveys and claims in the news. These skills are useful in almost every subject and in everyday decisions.

posts.name: Omar
posts.text: First-year programmes are already crowded. Departments should decide which quantitative skills their own students need instead of imposing one course on everyone.

requirements: State and support your position on a required data-literacy course.
Respond meaningfully to both Sara and Omar.
Develop a concrete course design or example in at least 100 words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Universities should require a short data-literacy course, but it should be flexible enough to avoid the problem Omar identifies. Sara is right that students in every field encounter graphs, averages and survey results, and misunderstanding them can lead to poor academic and personal decisions. However, a full semester of identical material could crowd an already demanding programme. A better design would be a six-week common module followed by examples chosen for each discipline. Physics students might examine measurement uncertainty, while history students could evaluate demographic records and biased samples. Students who already demonstrate the skills through a diagnostic task could complete a more advanced project instead. This model establishes a shared foundation without pretending that every major uses data in exactly the same way.
explanation: The response supports a requirement while directly addressing curriculum pressure through a short common module and discipline-specific applications.
The diagnostic option adds a concrete safeguard for students who already possess the basic skills; it is a proposal, not a claim about an existing university.
data literacyは『データを読み、評価し、使う力』、biased sampleは『偏りのある標本』です。モデルは唯一の正解ではありません。
phrases: establish a shared foundation — 共通の基礎を築く
discipline-specific applications — 専門分野別の応用
exercises.answerBasis: Original practice exercise; answer and explanation reviewed editorially. 解答・解説は編集作成。

exercises.title: 過去の送信を強く否定する
exercises.prompt: Could the assistant have sent the final file yesterday?
exercises.modelAnswer: The assistant can't have sent the final file yesterday.
explanation: Can't have + past participle expresses a strong conclusion that a past action did not happen. Sent is the required past participle.
Can't send would describe present ability or possibility, not a conclusion about yesterday.
can't have sentは『送ったはずがない』です。past participle（過去分詞）をhaveの後に置きます。

exercises.title: 点検前に修理を手配する
exercises.prompt: What service did you arrange before the inspection?
exercises.modelAnswer: We had the laboratory door repaired before the inspection.
explanation: Have + object + past participle means arrange for another person to perform a service. The door receives the repair.
Had the door repair would incorrectly make the door perform the action; repaired is required.

exercises.title: 過去に不要だった持参物
exercises.prompt: Was a printed ticket necessary for visitors?
exercises.modelAnswer: Visitors did not have to bring a printed ticket.
explanation: Did not have to + base verb means an action was unnecessary in the past. Bring stays in the base form after did.
Must not would mean the action was prohibited, which changes the meaning.
did not have to bringは『持ってくる必要がなかった』です。禁止ではなく不要を表します。
phrases: did not have to bring — 持参する必要がなかった

exercises.title: 発表予定を受動態で述べる
exercises.prompt: When do people expect the revised timetable to appear?
exercises.modelAnswer: The revised timetable is expected to be published next Monday.
explanation: The reporting passive uses subject + is expected + to-infinitive. A passive infinitive is needed because the timetable receives the action publish.
Is expected to publish would incorrectly suggest that the timetable publishes something.

exercises.title: 人にしてほしくないことを伝える
exercises.prompt: How can you politely ask someone not to move the equipment?
exercises.modelAnswer: I would rather you did not move the equipment.
explanation: Would rather + person + past simple expresses a present preference about another person's action. The past form makes the request less direct.
Would rather you do not move is not the standard pattern tested here.
would rather you did not ...は『あなたには〜してほしくない』です。丁寧な現在の希望を表します。

exercises.title: 助言を間接話法で伝える
exercises.prompt: What advice did the tutor give your group?
exercises.modelAnswer: The tutor advised us to compare the two explanations carefully.
explanation: Advise + person + to-infinitive reports advice directed at someone. Carefully naturally modifies compare.
Advise us compare omits the required to, while advise to compare omits the person receiving the advice.

exercises.title: 講義開始直後の出来事を倒置で表す
exercises.prompt: When did the fire alarm ring?
exercises.modelAnswer: Hardly had the lecture begun when the fire alarm rang.
explanation: Fronted hardly triggers inversion: hardly had + subject + past participle. When introduces the event that followed almost immediately.
Hardly the lecture had begun lacks the required auxiliary-subject inversion.
Hardly had ... when ...は『〜するとすぐに…した』です。inversionは『倒置』です。

exercises.title: 経験不足との対比を示す
exercises.prompt: Did her limited experience prevent her from finishing?
exercises.modelAnswer: Despite having little experience, she managed to complete the task.
explanation: Despite is followed by a noun phrase or -ing form, not a finite clause with although. Manage is followed by a to-infinitive.
Little modifies the uncountable noun experience and emphasizes that the amount was small.
despite having little experienceは『経験がほとんどないにもかかわらず』です。
phrases: managed to complete — 何とか完了した

exercises.title: 大きな反響の結果を示す

exercises.modelAnswer: The project attracted so much interest that registration closed early.

So many interest is incorrect because many modifies countable plural nouns.
so much interest that ...は『非常に大きな関心を集めたので〜』です。

exercises.title: 自習室の予約重複を報告する
exercises.subject: Study-room booking problem
exercises.context: You arrived for a study-room booking, but another group was already using the room. Write to Library Services. This is an imagined practice situation.
requirements: Identify the date, time and room you booked, and state what happened when you arrived.
Explain what library staff told you and mention the booking confirmation you can provide.
Ask the library to investigate and suggest how you can avoid or resolve the problem next time.
exercises.modelAnswer:
Dear Ms. Patel,

I am writing about my booking for Study Room 3 at 3:00 p.m. on 28 October. When my project group arrived, another group was already using the room and said that they had booked the same time.

The staff member at the desk told us that both bookings appeared in the system, but no alternative room was available. I still have the confirmation email and can forward it if that would help your investigation.

Could you please check how the duplicate booking occurred? I would also appreciate advice on how to confirm a room before arriving or what to do immediately if the same problem happens again.

Thank you for your help.

Best regards,
Alex Morgan
explanation: The message supplies the exact imagined booking details and explains the conflict without blaming the other group or the staff member.
It offers useful evidence and makes two connected requests: an investigation and practical guidance for a future problem.
duplicate bookingは『二重予約』、forward a confirmation emailは『確認メールを転送する』です。日付・氏名・予約は架空設定です。
phrases: Could you please check how ... occurred? — どのように〜が起きたか確認していただけますか。
I would appreciate advice on ... — 〜について助言いただけると助かります。

exercises.title: 期末試験とプロジェクト・ポートフォリオ
exercises.context: Should universities replace some final examinations with project portfolios? Explain your position.

posts.name: Maya
posts.text: A portfolio shows how a student's work develops over time and can assess research, revision and practical skills that a timed examination may miss.

posts.name: Leo
posts.text: Final examinations are completed under the same conditions, so they can be easier to compare. Portfolios may involve unequal access to time, equipment or outside help.

requirements: State and support your position on replacing some final examinations.
Respond meaningfully to both Maya and Leo.
Propose a concrete way to keep portfolio assessment fair in at least 100 words.
exercises.modelAnswer: Universities should replace some final examinations with project portfolios, but not in every course. Maya correctly points out that a portfolio can reveal research, revision and problem-solving processes that disappear in a two-hour test. This is especially useful in design, writing and laboratory courses. Leo's concern about comparability is important, however, because unlimited outside help or expensive equipment could create unfair advantages. A fair system could require students to submit dated drafts, explain major revisions, and complete a short oral defence of their work. Departments could also provide the necessary software and equipment on campus. A smaller supervised test could remain part of the final grade when individual knowledge must be verified. This mixed approach would assess sustained work while preserving a common check on what each student can do independently.
explanation: The response supports partial replacement, uses each student's argument, and adds safeguards rather than treating portfolios and examinations as an all-or-nothing choice.
Dated drafts, an oral defence and shared equipment are concrete ways to verify authorship and reduce unequal access. The proposal is an example, not the only valid answer.
portfolioは『学習成果物集』、oral defenceは『口頭での説明・質疑』、comparabilityは『比較可能性』です。
phrases: reveal a student's development over time — 学生の成長過程を示す
preserve a common check — 共通の確認方法を維持する
exercises.answerBasis: Original practice exercise; answer and explanation reviewed editorially. 解答・解説は編集作成。
